**iv**   
**Testimonials and Endorsements** 

When David mentioned that he was authoring a book on “saving  your house,” his only comment was “Hope you are not too  shocked…” Frankly, I wish I was. Miser or mogul, it seems that  everyone is going to feel this downturn if they don’t already. Just  today a friend confided that he doesn’t know how he’s going to  make his mortgage payment in four days. He and his wife both  have PhDs and they live in a very modest home. Apparently no  one is immune. Therefore, this is not a book about *them*. It’s a  book about *us*. David and Craig have compiled an excellent  resource that can only be written by someone who has gone  through the agony and is willing to talk about it with candor and  transparency. 

This is not your parents’ real estate market. I recently read that  there is no longer a need for the neutron bomb. We already have  something that destroys people and leaves buildings intact. It’s  called a *mortgage*\! But the practical insights in this book can help.  You are fortunate to have a copy in your hands. Take the wisdom  of *42 Rules* to heart and then pass it along to a friend. They’ll  thank you for it. As an entrepreneur who is working on rule \#43,  I should know. 

Rick Heggem   
Founder, Primarq Inc.

Intro

**My Story: David**    
**Coleman** 

My story starts back in late 2002, when I refinanced    
our home to do some significant repairs and addi   
tions. I added a two-car garage and a second bath   
room. I replaced wood flooring in two bedrooms,    
and installed new cabinetry in the kitchen and    
upstairs bathroom. To create work-at-home space,    
I converted the old garage into an office (since the    
right-of-way to this building had been sold by a pre   
vious owner so it could no longer be used as a    
garage). I ended up putting more into the house    
than it originally cost. I bought the home 21 years    
ago for \$225k and refinanced the house several    
times for either a better rate or to make repairs and    
additions. 

Unfortunately, this was also a tough time for the    
high-tech industry, and things kept getting worse. I    
lost many of my clients and by 2003 reached a low    
in revenues. We ended up using up all our savings    
just to stay afloat. In 2003, I finally filed for bank   
ruptcy to help keep my house and deal with some    
of my business and credit card debt. I did a chapter    
13 bankruptcy and by July of 2007 had paid it all off.    
I had no debt. 

In the summer of 2007, we started looking to refi   
nance because my first mortgage was due to adjust    
in November and my mortgage broker said “oh the    
five year fixed 25 year adjustable should be no    
problem, just re-finance before the five years is up    
and get a fixed rate.” And I believed her. Initially, the    
refinanced mortgage was at a five year fixed rate of    
5.375%, and the monthly, interest-only payment  

**42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure 1**   
was \$2418.75; all payments were made under this rate for five years. In  November of 2007, the rate jumped to 7.5% and the monthly, interest-only  payment increased to \$3990.55, an increase of \$1571.80 per month,  which was more than we could afford. We used up whatever money we  had to pay this new higher mortgage rate and at the same time tried to  contact the mortgage company to explain the problem. 

After trying for several months, we finally talked with someone who said  we should talk to the people in the loan modification department. We  called an 800 number and two weeks later they sent us a loan modification  application. We filled it out, along with about 80 pages of supporting docu 

mentation, and sent it in during February of 2008\.  

We got a letter back saying they had received the application. We waited  about six weeks and heard nothing back. So I called the mortgage com pany, they said they were swamped with applications and it might take a  while for anyone to get back to me. So I waited for a few more weeks and  called back again only to find out that they had lost the application. After  talking with someone for almost an hour, I got them to send me another  application for loan modification. This one went in at the end of April 2008  and by June I still had not heard back from our mortgage company.  However, the mortgage company was also failing. 

Since I was getting nowhere, and being a smart and educated person,  I swallowed my pride and decided I needed help from an expert. I had this  happen once before when I applied for a building permit in San Francisco  to change a basement into a garage. After two years of fighting with the  city of San Francisco, my contractor threw in the towel and recommended  we get an “expediter.” We paid him \$1500 and in less than two months we  had our building permit. So I figured this was one of those situations. I went  on the Internet to look for someone with expertise to help. I talked to a  number of people, and particularly liked a woman I talked to in San Diego,  who was also a mortgage broker and sounded honest and sincere. 

It turned out I was a good judge of character but a bad judge of companies  to get help from. One clue I should have seen is that they wanted all the  money up front. If you give them all of it up front, you have no leverage,  which is where I found myself. 

I got a frantic call one evening from the mortgage broker saying that the  company she had worked for were crooks, and that she had 10 clients  here in California (the parent loan modification company was in Florida)  and that the company had done nothing on behalf of any of her clients.  Further she had found out that companies in Florida could not legally help  homeowners in California. So here we had paid \$2850, spent all this time  filling out forms again, and got nothing out of it.

**2 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
Now, to her credit, the mortgage broker used her own money to hire a  lawyer to sue the parent company because first, they had stopped her  commission check, and second, they had done nothing for any of her cli ents. I did talk to the lawyer on the phone and by e-mail a few times, and  sent her the documents she requested, but have not heard anything for  almost a year and never expect to see that money again. An expensive  lesson in not doing my homework\! 

At that point I still felt I needed help, but was not willing to pay anyone again  and was very wary of getting ripped off, yet again. I went to a nonprofit  organization in San Francisco that helped people with similar problems. I  spent a few hours with the counselor catching him up on what had gone  before. He assured me that he did these applications all the time and had  great success with loan modifications. So at the end of June, my third  application for a loan modification went into the mortgage company. I was  also told that if I kept paying the mortgage at the higher rate (7.5%) there  was no reason for the mortgage company to ever talk to me because I was  doing what they wanted. So I stopped paying my mortgage in hopes that  someone would look at my application and talk to me about a loan  modification. 

I had to endure an unending stream of collection calls and patiently  explained the situation to anyone that would listen. However, I soon  learned that these were low-level people just hired to try to collect what  monies they could and they had no authority or knowledge of how to do  anything else. So I unplugged our home phone. This whole process took  quite a toll on both my wife and me, and on top of all of this my dad died  suddenly at the end of April 2008\. I have not been sleeping well since, was  exercising only intermittently, went on antidepressants, and even had  days when I did not want to get out of bed. 

Finally, just before Christmas of 2008, I was fed up and since I got nowhere  in calling Washington Mutual (WaMu, who had been bought over the sum mer by Chase Manhattan), I figured I would call the CEO and Chairman  of the Board of Chase Manhattan and give him a piece of my mind. So I  found his number on the Internet and called. A real person actually  answered (someone on his staff, I never got to speak to the CEO). She  listened to my story patiently and said that she would see what she could  do, and that people at Chase really had no idea what the WaMu people  were doing. About two days later, I did get a response from WaMu asking  for additional information, information we had already sent them. I sent  that request along to the counselor at the nonprofit and he sent in the  documentation again. A few days later, just after Christmas, we got a letter  from WaMu denying our loan modification. The reason was we had too  many expenses.

**Intro 3**   
I then decided that I was never going to get anywhere without a lawyer, and  since they were going to take my house anyway, why not make it as painful  for the bank as possible. So instead of giving my money to the mortgage  company I gave it to a lawyer. That lawyer turned out to be Craig Triance,  who is the coauthor of this book. 

I called back the counselor at the nonprofit and told him I had received a  letter denying the loan modification. His response was “try to sell the  house and find someplace else to live.” He even referred me on to his girl  friend who was a real estate lawyer and she came to the same conclusion.  I have lived in this house for 21 years and would be damned if a bank was  going to take it from me because of some mistakes they had made that  messed up the whole U.S. economy with other industries falling like a row  of dominos. 

At that point, I thought it was a good idea to find out what my house was  really worth. We had it appraised (in the unsuccessful refinancing pro cess) in January of 2008 for \$1.1 million. The total of my two mort gages was about \$740, 000, so I thought I was OK—boy was I wrong\!  My real estate agent friend pulled some comps for me to see what other  houses like mine were selling for in my neighborhood (which was sup posed to have held up well compared to other neighborhoods in San  Francisco). I found out that the house had dropped in value \$200,000  in one year. But that it was worth about \$900,000. Unfortunately, I did  not want to sell the house or move, so I decided to try exploring some  other options. 

Early in December, my house was put into foreclosure by the new mort gage company. Did the mortgage company notify me, of course not\! I  found out about it by talking to someone from the mortgage company on  the phone, which I had called to see what I could do about paying my  mortgage at a more reasonable rate. 

She told me I was in foreclosure and that they could not accept any pay ments from me. This was a big shock to me, and eventually I did get a  written notification from the mortgage companies lawyers (trustee) that I  was in foreclosure. Evidently, when you file for foreclosure, it is a public  document. We were deluged with offers from real estate agents to sell the  house, from investors who wanted to buy the house (at a huge discount),  and lawyers who said they could help me with a loan modification. 

Although my consulting business was very busy at that time, I patiently  talked to them all, asked a lot of questions, and tried to educate myself  more on my situation. I eventually talked to a saleswomen for this lawyer  (who helped with loan modifications) who was very sharp and had an  accounting background. When I told her the whole story she asked me to  fax her not only my profit and loss (P\&L) statement but also the financial 

**4 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
forms we (with the help of the counselor at the nonprofit) submitted to  WaMu. I did, and a series of phone calls ensued with me, my wife, and the  saleswoman. She had looked through the documents and found some  discrepancies in our expenses (the exact thing that WaMu said we had too  many of the last time they denied our application). 

My wife is a bookkeeper and tax preparer and also works for our accoun tant, so she is pretty good with numbers. We went through all the numbers  again and the saleswomen came back to us and said that we had double  counted some of our expenses and that they were represented both on  the P\&L as well as the loan modification form. When we worked this out,  our expenses had dropped \$3000 a month. 

At this point, I was not stupid enough to call WaMu about this, so I called  the CEO of Chase Manhattan again (the women I had talked to before had  given me her number). I never did get to talk to her, but did complain vocif erously that WaMu had taken six months to respond to my application,  and then denied it, and that we had new financial information to give them.  Sure enough, two days later I got two calls from WaMu, one from the  supervisor of the negotiator who had denied our loan modification. The  calls gave me a fax number to send in the new documentation and that  they would consider it. Of course I faxed the documentation they requested  in just before 2008 ended. I did get a letter back promptly from the WaMu  negotiator for my mortgage saying that they were reviewing my applica 

tion, that this review did not stop the foreclosure process, and was no  guarantee of a successful application. Finally, for the first time in a year,  after two calls to the CEO, WaMu had actually responded to me. 

But I was not very trusting of WaMu and their process, so I did agree to  hire the lawyer to review my case and see if there was enough merit to  fight WaMu and save my house. 

By now you are probably exhausted just reading this saga, but it is not  over. I talked with a paralegal in the lawyer’s office, who had taken an  afternoon and carefully reviewed all of the documents we sent. We not  only sent the 80 pages that went with our WaMu application, but all of the  original loan documents for both mortgages. The lawyer was going to do  a forensic audit of all of the documents to see if the mortgage company  had made any mistakes in the mortgage documents and the mortgage  process itself. 

In the mean time, my consulting business had been doing well (2008)  was one of my best years since 2000\. However, my credit score with my  bankruptcy and the reports of late or nonpayment on my mortgage had  dropped to the 500s (which is terrible), but not something I was going to  worry about because I never expected anyone to give me credit (for any 

thing) ever again. I was now in a cash, rather than a credit economy.**Intro 5**   
I started putting money in the bank (after paying off the rest of the bills we  owed). The lawyer’s representative, whom we talked with first, said we had to  reduce our debt, and suggested that my wife call the credit card companies  and negotiate with them to get our debt down. I did not have any credit cards  or debt, after my bankruptcy, but my wife, who had racked up a lot of credit  card debt (separate accounts), is not a great negotiator and so was not very  successful in dealing with the credit card companies. 

We wrote a new hardship letter detailing what we had been through and  that we wanted to save our house and wanted to talk with the mortgage  company about how we could do that. At this point, we owed them about  \$30,000 in back mortgage payments, and their only response was “send  us the \$30,000 or we will take the house through foreclosure.” Not exactly  an organization willing to work with us. I did not have \$30,000 lump sum  they wanted to get me back into my mortgage and out of foreclosure. I  wondered if they might settle for some lesser amount and renegotiate the  terms of our mortgage. We did not want to be in an ARM (Adjustable Rate  Mortgage – described later) because as soon as rates went up again we  would be back in the same position. With all of the news about banks fail ing and all the foreclosures in California (and the rest of the country), I  thought (wrongly) that the bank would want to preserve a customer willing  to pay rather than foreclose on the house. A foreclosed house not only  costs the bank money, but the bank’s trustee would auction it off for even  less than the loan value, compounding their loss. No wonder the banks  were going out of business. I would too if I did business like that. The only  reason I could figure out was that the bank wanted a tax loss, but I turned  out to be wrong again. 

In the meantime, we were now late on our second mortgage and that com pany started calling again, 5–10 times a day. I did talk to the collections people  and told them that we were in foreclosure and that we were instructed by our  lawyer not to pay any mortgages until we got the situation resolved. However,  the second mortgage company kept calling many times a day. Finally, out of  frustration I asked the person on the phone why they kept calling and that I  was already in foreclosure. Their response (which I should have expected)  was “it was company policy to keep calling until they got the money.” I again  unplugged my home phone, blocked their number on my cell phone, and  would not take their calls on my work phone. I also called and e-mailed my  lawyer about this situation. Since I had given him power of attorney, I was  hoping he could help deal with the constant calling, and my lawyer responded  by sending forms to both the mortgage companies to say that they were the  ones to contact about the mortgages. 

On a conference call with my publisher (I have written four books about  electronic collaboration), I happened to mention my situation with the  mortgage companies, and my frustrations. I jokingly said “I should write a 

**6 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
book about how to save my house.” Her response was “how soon can you  get it in?” I was shocked, and stammered a response about I would think  about it and get back to her. I thought about it for a few days, and talked to  my wife and family, and decided that no one should have to go through  what we had gone through so far. Maybe by writing this book, it would be  cathartic and help me personally work out some frustration and also help  the many others that are in a situation similar to mine. I talked to my lawyer  Craig, and enlisted him as a coauthor in the book project. We went over  what was needed to produce this book quickly. We needed to each write  two rules a day to meet our publisher’s deadline. Since I am an expert on  collaboration tools (and Craig is not), I set up a wiki to support our interac tions and coordination of the writing for the book, and away we went\! 

I moved into my house on April 1, 1988\. As of the writing of this book  (21 years later), I am not sure if I will still be living in my house by the time  this book is published. Chase (who bought WaMu) did open “Homeowner  Centers” in early March, 2009 to start to deal with the mortgage problem  (much to their credit) and I met with a loan officer a few weeks ago. Not  only did I find out that I had qualified for a loan modification two times over  the last year, but that the investor that owned the loan had denied the  modification both times (Craig explains this well in his part of the introduc 

tion). What was even more ironic was the loan officer herself was trying to  get a loan modification (through another bank) and was going through the  same kind of frustrating process I was, so she was very empathetic. 

Admitting that my home is in foreclosure is embarrassing, and made me think  I was a fraud. But then I realized that it was just my shame talking. Keeping  silent only helped the mortgage companies and a banking system that is very  broken. It is my hope that you find my story appalling and that if you are in the  same situation, that it gives you hope and maybe a few ideas in how to save  your own house. To keep up with this evolving situation please see my blog  at: http\://www\.42rules.com/saving\_ house\_blog/ 

**Craig’s Story** 

I began my legal career in 1992 at a plaintiff personal injury firm. After a  few months of that, I got a job with a sole practitioner who represented  about 15 companies in the downtown Los Angeles garment district. I was  there for two years and learned street corner law—that is, piracy and buc 

caneering. After two years, my boss retired from the law to sell golf socks.  Really\! 

I went out on my own and had a probate/real estate/business litigation  practice in San Dimas, California. It was quiet and close to home. I did  some real-estate investing during this period and accumulated some 

**Intro 7**   
rental properties. I followed the real-estate market in southern California  closely and by the early 2000s, realized that things were askew. 

In 2002, I attended Foreclosure training with Ward Hanigan in San Diego,  Califonia. If you are ever interested in doing foreclosure work, you need to  attend Ward’s training in San Diego. There is simply no comparison any where in the world with what you learn there. I took away two valuable  lessons from that class; first, how to do my own title examinations work,  which ended up saving a few of my clients many thousands of dollars; and  second, people in foreclosure need help, and they are preyed upon. 

Ward taught us that telephone calls and mail were a waste of time, and if  you wanted to speak to people in foreclosure, you had to knock on their  doors. The deal was simple. They would move out, you would take over  their payments, renovate the house, and sell it at a profit. You and the  homeowner split the profits 50/50. 

I soon learned that most of the people we contacted were interested in  staying in their houses, but were not willing to help themselves. We were  told time and time again that they were not interested in selling their homes,  but were interested in getting a loan. My business partner at the time and  I saw a need, obtained the necessary licenses, and began writing loans  with the help of a long time processor who kept us out of hot water. 

Once you begin to write loans, you get bombarded by lenders offering  their products. As we looked at the various loan products, it became clear  that many of them were simply dangerous for the homeowner. The busi ness decision was made to sell only “hard money” loans and 30 year fixed  rate product. A hard money loan is based on the equity of the property. A  30-year fixed rate loan is the mortgage your mom and dad got. 

We did not write that many loans. We were careful and conscientious, and  I am proud to say that none of the loans we wrote have ever gone bad and  none of the loans we wrote have ever resulted in a foreclosure. 

In late 2007, my mortgage company began to be contacted by borrowers  who heard I was an attorney and they needed help with their mortgages.  I began to review their mortgage files looking for an angle to see if any of  these loans could be refinanced or altered. I began to find many violations  of federal and state lending laws, and began to write letters requesting  loan modification based upon violations of state and federal law. 

For most of the first half of 2008, the main response I got back from lend ers on loan modification was to ask “how many stories the building my  office occupied was.” I told them the building was four stories, and I was  then advised to jump off the roof head first. This went on for a few  months.

**8 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
In the spring of 2008, many of the lenders realized that I would not go  away and they had a serious problem on their hands, and attempted to  begin to modify loans. Loan modification has now become a cottage  industry. This book is being written to expose the readers to what goes on  behind the closed doors of these lenders and mortgage companies. 

Since early 2008, I and my staff (an awesome group) have modified a few  hundred loans and have saved our clients many hundreds of thousands  of dollars. We are not successful every time, but our overall percentage is  quite good. 

I want to take a few paragraphs here to describe how the mortgage busi ness has changed from what your mom and dad’s mortgage company did  and what the industry has done since 2000\. 

When mom and dad bought a house, they went to the local bank, filled out  an application, and waited. The local bank reviewed the application,  obtained additional documents and went to a loan committee. The loan  committee would examine mom and dad’s entire scenario, and would  approve or deny the loan, based upon experience and their analysis of  mom and dad. The process was slow and careful. It had to be, because  the bank was basically investing in mom and dad and the house for the  next 30 years. Most of the loans were either held by the bank for a long 

term investment, or in some cases were sold to either Ginnie Mae of  Freddie Mac if the loan met their criteria. 

In the early 2000s, the business model changed. The “mortgage-backed  security” or the “collateralized debt obligation” was introduced. This was  an entirely new way of selling mortgages to a secondary market. If you  wonder why modifying a loan is difficult, you will understand once I explain  the process. 

Loans, many hundreds of loans, were packaged by a company, such as  Lehman Brothers, and resold on the secondary market as an investment.  The process worked generally as follows. Loans were gathered into  “pools” of loans, with an estimated market value at maturity. These carried  names like the “Deutsche Bank National Trust Company as Trustee under  pooling and servicing agreement dated as of December 1, 2006 securi 

tized asset backed receivables LLC Trust 2006-WM4 Mortgage pass  through certificates series 2006-WM4” (seriously, I am litigating against  these folks). 

The loans also produced an income stream, and the prospective investor  was sold an interest in the pool based upon the income stream and matu rity value. Within the pool, the loans themselves were divided into  “tranches”. These were loans of a similar underwriting criteria, interest  rate, etc. There are several tranches within a pool. The way the individual 

**Intro 9**   
investors are paid works as follows. Everybody in tranch A is paid from  revenues, and then the revenue flows to tranch B, etc., much like a  waterfall. 

The problem with this model is that the expected mortgage failure rate  was less than 1%. If the mortgage failure rate rose above 5%, the lowest  tranches don’t get paid. If the mortgage failure rate rises about 10%,  nobody gets paid. In reality, failure rates are usually higher than 1%. We  are tracking a pool where the expected failure rate is in excess of 50%. 

The individual pool loans were sold and resold to a variety of individual  and institutional investors. Sometimes the same loan was sold to more  than one person. It is not unusual to have five or six investors be required  to approve a loan modification. All the investors need to approve a loan  modification for it to succeed. If that does not happen, a loan modification  does not happen. Some investors are upset they have lost money, and are  not sympathetic. 

I am telling you this because the loan modification industry is in a constant  state of turmoil and programs appear and disappear; loan modifications  are approved or disapproved, pretty much at random. It is very frustrating  that what a lender will approve today is not something they will approve  tomorrow. Nor should you expect that by reading this book, you can do a  successful loan modification. It is not as simple and as easy as it sounds. 

As I write this in early February 2008, a loan modification takes between  90 and 120 days to accomplish, sometimes longer. It takes 2–3 hours per  file per day to communicate with the lenders on the status of things. Most  of that time is spent on hold. The turnover at the banks is high. What is  posted on the bank’s computer system is sporadic. What you are told one  day is not what you are told the next. They lose paperwork. They lose  entire files. 

Also bear in mind that some loans simply cannot be modified. 

I am assisting in writing this book to give an overview of the process to help  educate the consumer. With this information the consumer should be able  to ask the right questions, be able to spot a scam when they see one, and  to stay away. This is a “sea monkey” business. What appears on the box  top and what appears in your aquarium are two very different things. Ask  any little boy who bought a cube of sea monkeys.

**10 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
**Intro 11**  
Rule1 

**“Many of today’s  financial systems  are broken not  because the rules  are bad, but**  

**because the rules  can’t keep up with  the situation that  they are meant to  prevent.”**   
**Rules Are Meant to Be  Broken**

We live in an extraordinary time, like no other in our  country’s history. Through technology, information  is transferred and consumed more rapidly and con sequently many events now occur more rapidly.  I often see a posting about an airplane crash on  Twitter before any of the news stations has the  story on the radio or TV (older technologies). It  is these more instant technologies which have  (I believe) contributed to the large fluctuations we  have seen in the stock market and the mortgage  crisis of the last few years. 

It is this perfect wave of technology, lack of over sight by the last administration, and some fancy  footwork by homeowners that have turned a strong  economy that was built on the bedrock of single  homeownership into a house of cards, and a house  that is currently in foreclosure. It’s not that there are  no rules; there are plenty of rules, too many rules\!  But the rules still take a long time to make and get  through congress to become laws. In the mean time, the financial climate changes at the speed of  the Internet. Many of today’s financial systems are  broken not because the rules are bad, but because  the rules can’t keep up with the situation that they  are meant to prevent. 

A good analogy is the publishing industry and the  publishing process. When I wrote my first book in  1995, it took me most of a year to write the book  (630 pages) and then another year and a half for  the publisher to get the book through their publica 

tion process and released to the reading public.  

**12 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
My book was about collaboration technologies, which like mortgage terms  are changing so rapidly that the book was outdated before it was even  printed. 

When I wrote a book last year (on the same topic—new collaboration  technologies) with one coauthor, we started in May of 2007, the book was  done by October and available in print by February, 2008\. From start to  finish the process had gone from 2.5 years to 8 months. Much of this is  because of new collaboration technologies. A more extreme example  is this book. My coauthor Craig and I wrote the book in a few months, and  it was fast-tracked through the publishing process and by May was  available both as an e-book and print book. 

In writing this book, both Craig and I are breaking many rules. Since when  does a homeowner tell people about his financial failures and the details  of his foreclosure? Since when does a lawyer share his years of training  and expertise in a book that costs \$20? Since when has this country had  seven to nine million people in foreclosure and losing their houses to  banks that don’t really want them? 

Like the publishing industry, many of the rules that held for financial and  economic systems are broken and are not serving those they are meant  to protect, but rather are being used as a lever to pry people out of their  homes. Dealing with the banks on a daily basis and seeing these injus 

tices (from both the point of view of a homeowner and a lawyer) had got ten us frustrated enough with these broken processes to decide to write  our own rules. Our goal is to help the millions that have been caught in this  economic morass, that are also frustrated and not sure how to fight back  to save their homes.

**14 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**

**“From reviewing  lots of family**  

**financial**

**modifications, we  see the same  problems over  and over again.”**   
One of the themes of this book is personal re sponsibility. The public had a hand in creating the  problem, the public will have a hand in solving the  problem. 

This rule will not make a lot of sense without under standing the author’s (Craig Triance) world view.  Things will improve, and the economy will eventu ally recover. It will be a long hard slog to get there,  and things will get worse before they get better.  You need to be ready to ride out the hurricane we  are all facing. Use this situation as an opportunity  to improve the family financial situation. 

From reviewing lots of family financial packages  while doing loan modifications, we see the same  problems over and over again. Here are some  ideas to help you avoid the problems that have  tripped up many other families. Hopefully this will  help you avoid being a casualty. 

•  Household budgets don’t fail from a single major  blow. They fail by death from a thousand cuts.  Trim expenses and eliminate the unnecessary  early on—that means now. That means no gour 

met coffee, no designer goods, no eating out  three times a day, etc. 

•  Entertainment expenses are staggering. We see  satellite/cable television bills in excess of of \$150  per month. Do you really need the full package of  premium channels? 

•  Get rid of your credit cards. Shred them and stop  using them. Pay them off as best you can. See if  

**16 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
you can negotiate both the interest rate and principal amount with the  credit card company, they are now getting hit with the same financial  crisis the mortgage companies are and may be more willing to deal. 

•  Sell or donate expensive toys for what you can get for them and get rid  of them. Boats, jet skis, and collector cars are expensive luxuries you  don’t need right now. 

•  Car payments are a major problem. See if the car loan company is will ing to negotiate a better deal. If not, consider giving them up. In south ern California, it is not unusual to see a family spend more than \$1000  per month on car payments. Buy a used one for cash instead. 

•  If your rental property does not have positive cash flow, consider selling  or short selling it. Rental rates will drop in the coming hard times as  more and more units come on line. Don’t get caught short and plan on  rental rates dropping. 

•  Have a written budget and stick to it. We are dumbfounded by the num ber of families we see *who have no idea* what they spend their money  on. Know what you spend it on and how much you spend each month. 

•  Once you have a budget in place, go through it line by line and cut 10%.  Take that savings and put it in the bank. 

•  Haggle. Learn that prices are negotiable. Take advantage of the current  economic softness and negotiate prices. 

•  Renting is nearly always cheaper than owning. You may want to con sider selling or leaving your property and renting while the downturn  takes place. As said above, rental rates drop in a downturn due to the  number of available units. Take advantage of that situation and con sider renting. 

•  You need either a cell telephone or a land line. Not both. That saves  \$50–\$60 per month right there. 

Knowing what you owe, when it is paid, and what you make can give you  a big advantage when renegotiating your mortgage or getting a loan modi fication. Fortune favors the prepared, if a loan negotiator from the bank  were to call you today, would you know what to say to him, or would you  just take any deal he put on the table?

—George Santayana 

The economy is a mess, foreclosures everywhere,  banks failing, the jobless rate is up, and the home less rate is up. How did we get into such a mess  when eight years ago the government had a surplus  in the budget, the jobless rate was a few percent,  and your house’s value was rising at a steady rate? 

**The Genesis of the Problem** 

Over the last decade, we have seen a long  housing bubble (where prices continued to rise)  and then the bubble popped and splattered  all over the place. That splatter is the economic  crisis we have today. For a really good flow chart on  how the subprime mortgage crisis happened  and what all the contributing factors were, see  http\://www\.tinyurl.com/3wxqog1    

A crisis can come from a number of factors hap pening in the same time frame, and thus com pounding the effect of any one factor (think of the  perfect storm). A crisis can also happen from a  number of mistakes you made over time eventually  catching up with you (like mine did). 

1\. upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/1/13/Subprime\_ Crisis\_Diagram\_-\_ X1.png.

**18 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
In 2002, when I went to refinance, my mortgage broker talked me into a  five-year fixed ARM at a low, initial interest rate. I fell for it, and so did mil lions of others. This was my first mistake. 

This mistake was compounded by the fact that mortgage brokers and the  banks they were selling mortgages to people who really did not qualify to  buy them. But everyone wants the American Dream—owning a house.  There was a kind of conspiracy because the mortgage qualification rules  were relaxed. Often an application required “no stated income” (kind of  like the “don’t ask, don’t tell rule” in the armed forces) allowing people to  qualify for loans on homes they could not afford at standard mortgage  interest rates. 

When these low “teaser” rates adjusted to an often much higher rate (in  2006–2007) that the borrower could not pay for, that was one of the first  big cracks visible in our economic foundation. That is exactly what hap pened to me in November of 2007\. Of course when I went to talk to the  bank about the situation, the bank did not want to hear it. 

**What I Learned from This Mistake** 

•  Don’t count on things being much better in the future, that may not  happen. 

•  Five years sounded like a long time but in the context of a mortgage it  wasn’t. 

•  Don’t let people talk me (or you) into loans I fundamentally have a prob lem with, no matter how low the “teaser” rate is. 

•  Don’t believe the “you can always refinance in a few years and maybe  at a lower rate” line; that too may not happen. 

•  You may never understand the bank’s reason for doing things, it may  seem illogical and even stupid to you, but they would not keep doing it  if they did not get something out of it. Don’t assume the bank’s reasons  for the mortgage are in line with your reasons for the mortgage. 

•  Once you put your money in you lose your leverage and become an  account number. 

•  The left hand almost never knows what the right hand is doing (don’t  expect different departments in the same bank to have talked to each  other about your situation). 

•  Figure out if the mortgage is good for you, or good for them. You could  be in a mortgage for 30 years, and so you are establishing a long-term  relationship with that lender. Make sure you can live with the terms of  the relationship because it is not so easy (or inexpensive) to switch to  another bank (and they may be worse).

**Rule 3: Learn from the Past 19**   
Rule4 

**“The problem with  this type of loan is  that the borrower  was qualified**  

**(if at all) only for  the low payment  *not* the higher  payment. So**  

**when the payment  resets, the typical  borrower faces a  30% shortfall in  household funds  to make the**  

**house payment.”**   
**What’s in Your Loan  Paperwork CAN Hurt  You**

The mortgage crisis is “contained” only in the sense  that Hurricane Katrina was “contained” to the Gulf  Coast. It has spread everywhere. In Appendix C is  an explanation of the type of loans which have pro 

duced the problem and where these loans were  written. This rule will tell you about the underwriting  criteria used. 

Loans are either adjustable or fixed. A fixed loan  means that the amount of the loan and the amount  of the interest to be paid is determined by the par ties to the loan in advance. These figures are  plugged into a financial calculator, and a payment  plan is determined. The payments remain constant  over the life of the loan. A fixed rate mortgage, for  example, has the same monthly payment in year 1  as it does in year 30\. This is the mortgage your  parents are familiar with. 

A variable rate loan has an interest rate that  changes over the life of the loan. The interest rate  is linked to a publicly available interest rate called  an index. Several indexes are used, the most com 

mon being the fed funds rate and the LIBOR  (London Interbank Overnight Rate) which is basi cally the fed funds rate for European banks. You  can find the index rate online or they are published  daily in the *Wall Street Journal*. 

The next step in the process is to add an additional  amount, called a spread, on top of the index rate.  

**20 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
The spread is determined by your FICO score (defined later) the loan’s  underwriting program criteria, and the incentives offered by the bank to  the loan officers at the time the loan is written. The spread can range from  nothing to 5%. 

To figure out what your loan’s interest rate is, add the index to the spread  and the sum is the loan interest rate. This interest rate can be adjusted  monthly, quarterly, or annually, depending upon the terms of your loan. 

Loans can then be made more complex by adding different payment  choices. These loans are called “option ARM loans” or “pick a pay loans.”  The four payments are selected by the borrower, and paid monthly. It is  perfectly permissible to vary the payments from month to month, so your  payment changes from month to month. 

Your choices of payment are (1) a negative-amortizing rate (discussed  below), (2) an interest only rate, (3) a 30-year fixed rate, and (4) a 15-year  fixed rate. The payment amount is lowest to highest in the order the  choices are presented. Most people opt for the negative-amortizing rate,  which is the lowest payment. 

That is because people are people and everybody likes a bargain. It is also  because if the borrower was qualified for the loan at all, they were qual ified for the negative-amortizing rate. In English, the borrower was  approved for the loan only on the lowest payment available. Normally,  30% or so of the household income is devoted to the mortgage payment.  When the payment increases and the household income does not, people  simply run out of money. 

The problem with the negative-amortizing rate is this. Each month, the  difference between that payment and the 30-year fixed rate payment is  added back into the loan. Your loan balance actually increases every  month you make this kind of payment. Not a good plan\!

**Rule 4: What’s in Your Loan Paperwork CAN Hurt You 21**   
Rule5 

“**What happened  then is that**  

**the federal**  

**government**  

**stepped in and  assumed all the  risk on behalf of  the public at large.  Whether or not  this was a good  investment is still  very unclear**.”   
**Confronting Moral  Hazard**

This is an excellent opportunity to address the con cept of moral hazard. Moral hazard is the concept  that a party protected from risk will behave differ ently from a party not protected from risk. The sys tem over the past few years has divorced lending  practices with repayment practices and created the  mess we currently have by encouraging risky  behavior in that investors or the government will  ultimately write the checks. 

The idea originated in the insurance industry, but is  commonly found in the finance industry as well.  The problem of moral hazard changes drastically  decision making on the finance level as well. Moral  hazard arose in the finance industry as follows. 

Mortgage salespeople were not using their own  money to fund mortgages; they were using bor rowed funds supplied by banks. This moved the  risk of loan failure from the mortgage sales people  to the banks. The banks then sold the loans to  investors shifting the risk from the banks to the  investors. The investors then sold the loans to  investment banks, shifting the risk to the invest ment banks. (Investors and investment banks are  two related but very separate entities.) The invest ment banks then sold portions of the mortgages in  small pieces to a different group of investors, mov ing the risk along to that group. Risk was passed  like a baton in a relay race; the last person to  hold the baton took all the risk. What happened  then is that the federal government stepped in and  

**22 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
assumed all the risk on behalf of the public at large. Whether or not this  was a good investment is still very unclear. 

**An Example of Moral Hazard in Everyday  Life** 

In your neighborhood are two houses. One was purchased using a stated  income 100% down loan with toxic financing and the loan resets within five  years to double the house payment. The other was purchased at 20%  down with a 30-year fixed rate mortgage, and the payments have been  made timely. 

In the mortgage bailout world we are about to experience, House One  will get all kinds of assistance and breaks as the government works to  prevent further foreclosures. The 30-year fixed rate mortgage holder will  be offered nothing, no assistance. 

Now consider this. House One forecloses and now becomes the low price  leader in the neighborhood (in most of the country, REO \[real estate  owned\] property set the prices). House Two’s owners are now upside  down (they owe more on their property than the mortgage amount) on  their properties and nobody will help them. Their only real choice to obtain  relief is to sell their home at a loss or walk away. Think this does not go on?  It goes on every week at open houses in Southern California—people  being punished for following the rules. What kind of message does that  send? 

Maybe it is time to send a message. Write an e-mail or a letter to your  congressperson or senator advising them that dumping an unlimited  amount of money on fixing the housing crisis is maybe not so good an idea  and is actually making the problem worse.

**Rule 5: Confronting Moral Hazard 23**   
Rule6 

**“Your job is to  make sure that  your situation fits  into one of the  categories that  Washington is  likely to deal with  in their fix-it plan.”**   
**Focus on Your Own  Situation**

You need to focus on your personal mess. Your  situation alone will not fix the system. Focus on fix ing your particular problem. Leave the big picture  to people who like to appear on C-SPAN. 

The best way for you to focus is to be prepared and  professional in your dealings with the banks. Be  prepared, have documentation, and concentrate  on the matter at hand. A little negative publicity, dis 

cussed in other rules, certainly helps, but by no  means makes your cause a crusade. 

As you prepare to fight to keep your house, you  need gather the information needed: 

•  Prepare a household budget. List all of the  income, and the entire outflow. Where do you  spend your money? There are also a number of  programs on the iPhone and Blackerry that can  help you keep a daily log of expenses. 

•  A simple way of showing that is to buy a small  spiral notebook and carry it with you everywhere  you go. When you spend money, write it down.  Go through the notebook at the end of the month  and you will be amazed at the few dollars each  day that just vanish. 

•  Find the paperwork from when you bought or  refinanced the house. It will be around some where. You will need all of the paperwork for your  forensic audit, which is discussed later in the  book. So go to the bank, fire safe, or wherever  you keep the paperwork and pull it out. 

**24 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
•  Next, you will need your last two year’s tax returns, and the supporting  documentation. The federal return along with the W-2, 1099, etc. should  be fine. Make copies. 

•  You will then need three month’s bank statements. You will need three  month’s bank statements from each bank account you have–that is,  checking, savings, etc. Make copies of the statements for whoever will  be helping you in this situation and for the bank. 

•  You will then need two month’s paycheck stubs. These need to be your  most recent paycheck stubs, not a random selection from last year.  Again, make copies. 

•  Then find your fire insurance policy. If you don’t have fire insurance on  your house, the lender will do what is called “forced placing” of a policy  and buy one for you. You can nearly always find your own policy much  more cheaply. 

•  Next, find your most recent property tax bill. If you property tax is  current, great. If not, know that the lender will pay the property tax and  bill you for the amount. So it helps a lot to know what the tax pay ments are. 

•  Finally, you will need the most recent loan statement for your home  mortgage. This will show who the servicing company is and the loan  number. The loan will have changed hands several times during its life,  so you need to know your most recent servicer’s information for contact  purposes. You will need to know the loan number as well. 

Once you have all this information, go to a local office supply store and find  an expandable file large enough for all of this information. You want all of  these papers in one, single spot. When you talk to the bank, go see a  counselor or attorney, or whatever, take this file with you. Do not leave the  file with anyone; have them make copies of what they need.

**Rule 6: Focus on Your Own Situation 25**   
Rule7 

**“It will be**  

**convenient to  have a name for  the ideas which  are esteemed at**  

**any time for their  acceptability, and  it should be a  term that**  

**emphasizes this  predictability.  I shall refer to  these ideas**  

**henceforth as the  conventional  wisdom” (John  Kenneth**  

**Galbraith, *The  Affluent Society*)**.   
**Conventional Wisdom  Will Not Help You**

The conventional wisdom is that your lender should  step in early to assist you before you run into trou ble, and will meet you with open arms to provide  assistance to you in restructuring your loan. That is  unfortunately not true. Nor is it true that most loan  modifications end up being successful. 

Most lender’s loss mitigation departments triage  borrowers. Triage is a medical term in which, in a  disaster situation, medical professionals concen trate their efforts on victims who can be saved with  intervention. Those victims who cannot be saved  due to the extent of their injuries, or are not badly  injured, receive little care. In lender practice, lend ers do not pay much attention to you until you are  behind in your payments. They are not interested in  assisting you proactively simply because (1) they  are inundated with requests for people who are  seriously behind and have only limited resources  and (2) most loan modifications proposed do not  work and people end up back in default. 

In the first situation, the sheer number of calls,  paperwork, e-mail, and borrowers in trouble pretty  much prohibit requests and files being handled  expeditiously. In addition, increasing the size of  loss mitigation and loan workout divisions are a  cash drain on the lenders. The lenders themselves  are under significant financial pressure as losses  mount. They are, through sheer business sense,  going to limit the resources expended on loan work outs because they see no profit in it and it is an  increase in overhead. Loan modifications and this  

**26 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
crisis have a limited run time, probably two or three years. By that time,  there will be massive changes to the banking system, either through con solidation, nationalization, or regulatory oversight and the problem will be  resolved by a combination of those factors. 

In the second situation, most loan modifications simply kick the can down  the road. A common problem is that the unpaid principal, interest, prop erty taxes, and insurance are rolled into the existing loan amount. The  payment is then computed from the new principal amount, which in creases. In addition, the lender will impose an impound account to make  sure that taxes and insurance are paid by the borrower going forward.  These numbers are divided by 12 and then added to the payment. The  net result is a situation in which, even though a loan has been modified,  the monthly payment actually increases. 

The conventional wisdom needs to grasp the concept that for real estate,  the years 2003–2007 represented an aberration likely never to be  repeated, for good reason. An effective loan modification for all loans writ ten in this time period is a complete rewrite of the loans using normal  lending standards, like the standard 31%–38% debt to income ratios to  reflect true borrower income. This will also require principal reductions on  loan balances. 

So consider this—a loan is restructured to reflect the true market value of  the house. The loan value is then computed based on that market value.  This drops the payment to an affordable level. The principal balance,  whatever it is, is then shifted to a second position type mortgage and a lien  against the house. As the market recovers, or if the borrower is able to sell  or refinance, the lender is repaid the principal balance. This protects the  lender and gives the borrower the chance to sell, refinance, or stay in the  house. There you go.

**Rule 7: Conventional Wisdom Will Not Help You 27**   
Rule   
8   
**Watch Out for Yourself**

**“Understand that  none of these  people are**  

**looking out for  you or even have  your best interest  at heart.”**   
There is a sucker born every minute. 

—W.C. Fields 

You can bet if there are millions of homeowners  today having problems with their mortgage or fac ing foreclosure that there are people out there will ing to scam these desperate people out of whatever  they have left. 

I know this is true because I receive offers in the  mail every day for help in loan modification, refi nancing, immediate buying of my home, help in  selling my home, etc. Understand that none of  these people are looking out for you or even have  your best interest at heart. They are looking out for  \#1, themselves. Many were mortgage brokers who  over the last six to seven years made a killing, and  when the bottom dropped out of the mortgage mar ket they had to find some other way to earn an  income. Many left the mortgage (real estate) indus try. Many decided that since no one could get a loan  or refinance anymore that they needed to see  where they could apply their skills. 

Some of them are truly helping people with the  more difficult processes of loan modification, or  are syndicating investors to buy up distressed or  foreclosure properties. If someone is having a hard  time, there are always others willing to take advan 

tage of it. I see these commercials all the time  on late night TV (when I can’t sleep) extolling the  virtues of buying at foreclosure auctions, that you  can get a \$300,000 house for \$40,000 or just for  

**28 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
back taxes\! Come on people, if it was that easy and that profitable every one would be doing it. The only one making money here is the one who  has the commercial and is trying to sell you their full proof system for new  wealth. 

A good analogy is the 1849 gold rush. Once gold was found people flooded  into California looking to seek their fortunes and get rich. Very few struck  it rich by finding gold. Those who did get rich were the people like Levi (the  jeans maker) who sold pants to all of the miners and made their fortune  that way. 

I guess in my own way I am like one of those fools rushing in to get the  gold, only in this case I am trying to save my house from a banking and  economic system that is radically broken because of the greed of a few.  However, there are still sharks out there willing to take a bite out of me, no  matter how small a fish I am. 

**Steps to Save You More Pain** 

I made the mistake of looking on the Internet to find someone to help me  with my loan modification process, and because I was scared and in a  rush, I made an emotional choice and picked the person I felt the best  about, believing that they would never do me harm. I was right, she was a  nice and honest person, but the company she worked for had tricked her  also (she never got her commission check) and they were not nice people,  they were sharks. If I had bothered to do more investigation before I sent  in my money I probably could have avoided losing the \$2850 I lost in May  2008, so it was an expensive lesson. Before you give money to someone  to help you with loan modification 

•  Be sure to check them out thoroughly on the Internet, look at conversa tions people are having online about the company. 

•  Get a personal referral from someone you know and trust. Once you get  the referral 

•  Ask to speak to some of their clients.   
•  Look for any red flags when interviewing those clients (like they did not  return my calls, I was never sure they actually did anything). •  Give it a time limit. The banks will not wait forever. If your situation has  not changed in 90 days, you need to start asking some hard questions. 

It is your money and your house, be prudent in taking care of it. Even if you  swim with sharks it does not mean they have to take a bite out of you, after  all there may be bigger or slower fish they would rather eat\!

**Rule 8: Watch Out for Yourself 29**   
Rule9 

**“Losing your**  

**house is not a  Marlboro**  

**Man moment.  There is no need  whatsoever to  remain the strong  silent type and  ride into the**  

**sunset.”**   
**Talk About Your**    
**Situation**

According to bank figures, the bulk of homeowners  in trouble go “Dick Cheney,” lock themselves in  their bunker and are never heard from. One Wells  Fargo source told me Wells Fargo never hears from  70% of the households they foreclose on. No letter,  no phone call, no nothing. 

If you take nothing else from this book, take this:  You need to admit to and be willing to talk about the  fact you have a problem here. There is, if you look  for it, lots of help out there. Losing your house is not  a Marlboro Man moment. There is no need whatso 

ever to remain the strong silent type and ride into  the sunset. Instead, you need to face the fact that  you need help and you need to seek out that help. 

•  Pick up the phone.   
•  See a legal aid clinic worker.   
•  Talk to your local housing assistance office. •  When your lender calls, pick up the phone and  tell them you have a problem (if they keep harass ing you, see Rule 37). 

I periodically conduct public seminars on the fore closure crisis and people’s choices in it. After every  seminar, I am approached by people with ques tions about a specific situation. These people never  have a problem themselves. Instead, they have a  friend or family member who is in trouble. So find  the friend or family member willing to assist you in  getting through the problem. Have that person con tact someone on your behalf. Have that persons  

**30 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
come with you to the assistance office. (We get lots of parents in with their  adult children in our initial consultations.) BE WILLING TO TALK ABOUT  THE PROBLEM AND GET HELP. 

I close this rule with a better description of what you can do than anything  I can write instead. It is a passage from the famous poem by Dylan Thomas,  *Do Not Go Gentle*: 

And you, my father, there on the sad height, 

Curse, bless me now with your fierce tears, I pray. 

Do not go gentle into that good night. 

Rage, rage against the dying of the light. 

This is going to be the biggest financial crisis you will face in your life. You  don’t have to face it alone. Don’t face it alone. GET HELP\!

**Rule 9: Talk About Your Situation 31**   
Rule10 

**“I ran the wrong  kind of business,  but I did it with  integrity.”**  

**—Sydney Biddle  Barrows, in**  

**Marian Christy,  “‘Mayflower**  

**Madam’ Tells All,”  Boston Globe,  1986**   
**Go Public**

You have a huge advantage over the banks. They  are public companies and you are not. (At least they  are public companies as of March 2009; whether  or not banks stay that way remains to be seen.)  Consider doing one or both of the following: 

Public corporations are required to have share holder meetings. These take place on an annual  basis at the company headquarters. If you live near  a bank headquarters and have problems with your  loan, buy a share of stock, and as a sharehold er, attend the shareholder’s meeting. The shares  themselves are not expensive (Bank of America  shares currently trade for about the price of a Big  Mac, fries, and a Coke). You buy a share or two, and  viola, you are a shareholder. You get on the list of  shareholders and they mail you the annual report,  along with the announcement of when and where  the shareholders meeting will take place. 

On the appointed day, the board of directors assem bles, along with the senior officers of the bank.  Their part of the meeting drones on for some period  of time, so bring something to read. At some point  later in the meeting, the attending shareholders will  be asked if there are questions from the floor.  Here’s your chance\! 

Among the questions you can ask the esteemed  corporate leadership are: 

**32 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
•  Explain the use of special investment vehicles and how their use alters  the reported earnings of the corporation 

•  Ask what the bank’s exposure to derivative stock trades is, in real dol lars (the number will shock you) 

•  Closer to home, ask them to explain their home loan underwriting crite ria for what type of loan you have 

•  Ask them what their loss mitigation policy is to keep homeowners in  their homes 

•  Ask if there has been any training in the loss mitigation on how to apply  that policy, assuming one exists 

•  Ask why their federal government bank stress test grade is so low  (watch the news on this) 

At this point, security will ask you to leave. If things went well, you will be  on Bloomberg and MSNBC that night. And you made your point. 

Another alternative is to picket. Select your local bank branch, make up a  Day-Glo colored sign with a catchy slogan (my personal favorite is from a  protest on *Wall Street*: “Jump Already”). And start marching in a circle.  Make sure you are on the public sidewalk, as you can be arrested for pro 

testing on private property. If you choose to do this, you will draw attention.  Have some flyers handy to hand out, explaining your situation in a single  page the news reporters can take with them. A bullhorn or megaphone  works great to get attention if their use is allowed by local law. The quick 

est way to do that is to check with city hall. 

If you are a member of an organization, so much the better\! Make it an  organizational outing. My only protest march was greatly strengthened  when the local teamsters showed up (they are loud and they know how to  get attention). We were protesting the closing of a local manufacturing  plant and when the teamsters showed up, their chanting was very effec 

tive and rather pointed against specific members of company manage ment. The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) soon arrived in force,  and we wisely retired to a local bar when LAPD rather forcefully told us the  fun was over. 

The idea behind both of these strategies is to draw attention to your situ ation with someone who is in a position to do something about it. That  person is not the line cubicle worker in the call center. The point of the  protest is to find the manager with line authority over your problem. And if  you are shrill enough, that person will find you.

**Rule 10: Go Public 33**   
Rule11 

**“One of the**  

**reasons we are in  this credit crisis is  because many of  us lived beyond  our means, and  now the payment  is due.”**   
**Reduce Your Debt**

In a loan modification, the bank is looking for cer tain financial numbers. They are looking for a ratio  of debt to income and specifically what percentage  of your monthly income the mortgage might be.  Usually, they want it to be between 30% and 40%  (these rules are changing on a daily basis). They  also look at your monthly expenses. 

One of the ways to reduce your monthly expenses  is to look at your credit card debt. I too saw the  infomercials on TV that say “if you buy this book  and follow my plan, you can cut your credit card  debt enormously.” I bought the book, tried the plan,  and got nowhere with the credit card companies. 

Most of our credit cards were at the ridiculous inter est rates of 25%–32%. Loan sharks don’t even  change that much\! But it is legal for the credit card  companies to do so because they are based in  North Dakota where there are no usury laws, so  they can charge whatever interest rate they want.  Since their cost for borrowing money from the gov ernment is almost zero (0.25%), most of the inter est they are charging you is pure profit. 

Here is what happened when I called to try to  reduce our credit card debt. Out of four credit cards,  we got one company to reduce the rate from 25%  to 14.9%. They would not reduce the amount owed.  On the other three credit cards the bank just said  “no.” Not only did they say “no” but there was no  process to even talk to someone about it. I was told  to send a letter into a P.O. box address and they  

**34 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
would consider it. Translation: It goes into the round file and don’t expect  a response in your life time. 

In the past, the threat of bankruptcy would usually get you transferred to  a supervisor who did have the authority to make a change. But the banks  got the rules changed on bankruptcy and credit card debt in 2005, so you  no longer have the same protection you did. 

Today their response to your talking about bankruptcy is “that is your  option.” Not only that, but there was also no way to escalate the call to a  supervisor. When asked, the person we talked to said “they are in a differ ent location and are not available at this time.” The other response we got  was “our system is down please call back in 2–3 hours.” 

In Rule 12, Craig seems to have had better luck with his credit card com panies than I did in reducing the interest rate on his credit cards. It might  not be a coincidence that the same bank that holds my mortgage also  owns our credit card debt. 

**Change Your Behavior** 

After my bankruptcy finished in 2007, I chose to change my behavior.  I have no credit cards (in my name) and no debt (except my mortgages).  I choose not to get a credit card (even if there was a bank crazy enough to  give me one) because I know I will use it, and I will get back on the treadmill  the credit card company wants me on. The only situation I have run into  that requires a credit card (and will not accept a debit card) is a car rental  (sometimes a cash deposit can take care of this). 

Paying off the minimum amount on a credit card (which is calculated so  that you will never pay off the debt) with an interest rate of 32% has my  debt rising faster than I can pay it off. I will be on that treadmill forever, an  indentured slave to the credit card company; which is what they want. 

The other thing I had to do was to look at my spending behavior. Was I  living beyond my means? Believe me I have asked myself that question  everyday for the last two years. I have eliminated a lot of expenses from  my budget, and this is an ongoing process. 

One of the reasons we are in this credit crisis is because many of us lived  beyond our means, and now the payment is due.

**Rule 11: Reduce Your Debt 35**   
Rule12 

**“It is now not  unusual to also  see \$20,000–** 

**\$100,000 in credit  card debt, in**  

**addition to car  and mortgage  payments.”**   
**Don’t Rely on Credit  Cards**

A common theme for homeowners in trouble is to  use their credit cards to make their house payments.  Don’t play that game. 

You are substituting 5%–10% money for 12%–18%  money, or higher. Worse, you are shutting off a fi nancial safety valve by using credit cards to make  house payments. You may well need your credit  cards to survive in the event you lose your job going  forward. Think grocery money. 

If your house loan resets, or you lose your job, you  are now facing a waiting game. Unlike credit cards,  where the issuing bank can arbitrarily cancel or  change your ability to use the card, a mortgage  works differently. There is a preset time period  before the mortgage lender takes back the house.  Use that time lag to your advantage. 

Time after time we see people who are losing their  homes come in for a financial review when they  need a loan modification. It is now not unusual to  also see \$20,000–\$100,000 in credit card debt, in  addition to car and mortgage payments. This debt  load is simply crippling and badly impacts any  attempt to improve a family’s financial situation. 

If you have a massive credit card debt load, speak  to a bankruptcy attorney. The bankruptcy rules  were changed in 2005 to limit bankruptcy in credit  card situations. However, those rules were imple 

mented at the top of the housing market when it  was clear that most borrowers, based on home  equity, were solvent. Sadly, that is no longer the  

**36 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
case. If you are upside down on your home loan and you owe credit card  debt, you are most likely insolvent. 

A bankruptcy attorney can tell you whether or not you would qualify for a  bankruptcy. If you do, take a look at that option. This train of thought is  anathema to many people under normal circumstances. We are not in  normal circumstances. The rules are now different and desperate situa 

tions demand desperate measures. Getting out of credit card debt by  bankruptcy is something you should strongly consider. 

If you cannot or will not file bankruptcy, be proactive and contact your  credit card company. They are facing the same financial problems mort gage companies are facing. Their problem is that their debt is unsecured,  and will most likely be written off in massive amounts. This makes them  somewhat more flexible to deal with than mortgage lenders since their  options are much more limited. 

As with your mortgage lender, be candid and upfront and don’t lie to them.  Tell them you are having problems making your payments and need assis tance. They are often willing to reduce interest rates over the phone (the  author was able to reduce a credit card interest rate from 16% to 10%  simply by asking the customer service representative out of the blue). See  if they have forbearance agreements (agreed reduced payments for a  period of time to get back on your feet) or a deferred payment plan (no  payments for a set period of time, usually a few months). 

The other issue you need to keep in mind in running up massive credit card  debt is that there is an upcoming rule change on how credit card balances  are calculated and how billing cycles are controlled. That will mean higher  interest rates on credit cards. How high? Try 25%–35% interest rates. At  that rate, your payments will soar if you max out your cards. 

Play it safe and do not use your credit cards to make house payments.**Rule 12: Don’t Rely on Credit Cards 37**   
Rule13 

**“A common theme  with people**  

**unable to make  their house**  

**payments is to  max out credit  cards, then**  

**borrow from their  retirement**  

**account in an**  

**attempt to keep  the house.”**   
**Your House Can Eat  Your Retirement**    
**Account**

Your retirement account is for retirement. It is not a  rainy day fund. Leave it alone. 

Lots of people are facing a financial tipping point  now. Many more will join them in the next few years.  Don’t go over the edge. You have to save money.  One way to do that, tax-deferred, is your retirement  account. 

A common theme with people unable to make their  house payments is to max out credit cards, then  borrow from their retirement account in an attempt  to keep their house. Maxing out credit cards was  discussed in Rule 12\. The problem most frequently  seen is that they exhaust both of these resourc 

es. Their situation does not improve, and they lose  the house anyway. Once this happens, there is no  financial buffer of any kind to fall back on. 

Most banks, when evaluating you for a forbearance  agreement (an agreement for a reduced payment  for a stated period) or loan modification, don’t con sider retirement accounts as an asset. The reason  is that these accounts are less liquid than people  think. In the first place, you don’t just write a check  from the account. You must contact the account ad ministrator and request liquidation of the account.  This ranges from very easy with a few forms to fill  out to the equivalent of a root canal. 

The next issue is that the money you take from the  account is taxed. Under current rules, 10% of the  taxable money you withdraw is taxed as a penalty  

**38 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
for early withdrawal. This is in addition to paying income tax on the money  at your normal tax rate, since the distribution is taxable income. You need  to take the tax ramifications of your decision into consideration. If you do  not, you get a nice tax bill next April 15\. And the IRS is not a particularly  pleasant group to deal with. 

If you must take money out of your retirement account, do a quick figure  on the tax owed and put that money away somewhere and do not spend  it. You don’t want to owe the IRS money, so plan ahead. 

The better approach is to begin working with your bank, or seek assis tance, as you begin to run out of liquid cash (which David tried to do, but  he got nowhere). Be proactive and don’t simply throw money at the prob lem. As will be expanded in Rule 17 “Strategies for Uncommon Times,” we  are entering into an economic era in which cash will be king and credit will  be hard to come by. You need to plan for that reality. That means keeping  some cash on the sidelines—and your retirement account is a good place  for that. 

Also bear in mind that if you are sued by your creditors, your retirement  account cannot, in most cases, be attached or seized by your creditors.  O.J. Simpson is the most famous example of this loophole. Understand  that in this down cycle, there will be creditors who will sue you. Make the  law work in your favor and keep money in your retirement account. You  can’t touch it and your creditors can’t touch it. 

In addition, should you have to file bankruptcy, a portion of your retirement  plan is an exempt asset and is not subject to bankruptcy. Consult with a  bankruptcy attorney for the details.

**Rule 13: Your House Can Eat Your Retirement Account 39**   
Rule14 

**“We encounter a  fair number of  people with a very  decent, rational  mortgage, and a  HELOC for several  hundred thousand  dollars. The line  has now frozen,  and the borrower  is now looking at  a substantial**  

**monthly**  

**payment.”**   
**Home Equity Should  Not Be Spent on a Boat**

A home equity line of credit (HELOC) is a danger ous friend. Use for necessities, not luxuries. 

During the recent run-up in housing prices, many  homeowners opted to do either cash-out refinance  or obtain a HELOC. A cash-out refinance means  that a new mortgage is obtained in an amount  higher than the old one. The difference in the  amount is paid in cash to the homeowner. A HELOC  works essentially as follows. 

The HELOC creates usually a second position  mortgage or trust deed against your home. Instead  of the money coming to you all at once, you are  given what looks like a checkbook or perhaps a  debit card to draw money from the account. There  are typically minimum and maximum withdrawals  that you can make from the account. The docu 

ments recorded against your home as collateral  show the maximum value of the HELOC. There is  no way of knowing from the public record how  much of the equity line has been drawn down. 

The documents themselves have far broader pow ers reserved to the banks than a conventional  mortgage or trust deed. The documents give the  bank the power to adjust the interest rate, freeze  the credit line, or call the credit line, meaning they  have the right to ask for their money back. Right  now in the cycle, most credit lines have been either  cancelled or frozen. When that happens, the line of  credit becomes a second trust deed or mortgage,  with the principal balance representing the amount  

**40 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
drawn on the account and the interest rate is fixed by the agreement. You  essentially now have an amortized mortgage payment until the HELOC is  repaid. 

The major problem with the use of HELOCs in the last cycle is that they  were used essentially as a second job, or worse as play money. They were  used to by stuff—cars, boats, big screen TVs, trips to Hawaii, whatever.  They should not be used for that purpose. What they should be used for  is an emergency fund or a safety net. They should not be drawn against  except in the event of a family fiscal emergency. Needing a new car or a  cruise is not a family fiscal emergency. 

We encounter a fair number of people with a very decent, rational mort gage, and a HELOC for several hundred thousand dollars. The line has  now frozen, and the borrower is now looking at a substantial monthly  payment. The payment can exceed that of their original mortgage. The  HELOC is now the major source of household financial distress. Worse,  in final analysis, there is little to show for the use of the HELOC—it was  consumed, not invested. 

Because the bulk of HELOCs are second position trust deeds, and many  of them are secured against properties that are underwater, it is often  possible to negotiate favorable terms with the lenders to get the HELOC  payments reduced or compromised. Some lenders are willing to accept  flat lump sum payoffs of HELOC balances. Consider that negotiation  strategy in your dealings with your lenders. 

One day the fiscal crisis will pass and things will recover. Eventually  HELOCs will become available again. Don’t get one. Consider the idea  that having a free and clear house is better for you than having a  HELOC.

**Rule 14: Home Equity Should Not Be Spent on a Boat 41**   
**Section 2: Rules to**    
**Help you dig your way**    
**out**

This section is filled with practical rules to help you    
out of the current mortgage, foreclosure (or near    
foreclosure) situation you are in. It tells you how to    
cope during this crisis and gives you some strate   
gies for dealing with the bank, collection agencies,    
and scam artists. These rules encourage you to be    
persistent, vigilant, and detail oriented (because if
