you were all those things you would not be in this    
situation). This section’s rules give you some strat   
egies and help as groundwork for the third and final    
section which covers your options. 

**42 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
**Section 2: Rules to Help you dig your way out 43**  
Rule15 

**“Before you sit  down at the table,  the terms,**  

**amount, and**  

**interest rate of  your loan should  have been agreed  to. If there is no  agreement, do not  come to the**  

**table.”**   
**Check for Lender**    
**Mistakes**

Your first line of defense is reviewing what you are  signing—when you sign the documents. 

Everybody reading this book has gone through the  drill. You gather in an escrow office, an attorney  office, or even your kitchen table and the loan offi cer pulls out a huge pile of documents, and you  start signing. The loan officer is normally in a hurry,  and they want the signing done yesterday. Not so  fast. 

When you begin to shop for a loan, take notes.  Every conversation you have with your loan officer  should be documented. Most loan officers don’t  document their conversations, so that gives you a  leg up. Before you sit down at the table, the terms,  amount, and interest rate of your loan should have  been agreed to. If there is no agreement, do not  come to the table. 

From the huge stack of documents, you need to  really look at just four of them. But you need to  review those four very carefully. 

1.  *The settlement statement, or HUD-1*. This is the  balance sheet for the transaction. Every penny  coming into the transaction, and every penny  coming out of the transaction, needs to be doc 

umented here. Go through the settlement state ment line by line and question any charges.  A rough idea of what charges are and what they  should be are in Appendix E. *If you don’t like the  explanation of a charge, don’t sign*. Do not  

**44 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
believe an oral promise that the document will be fixed later. It will not.  Don’t sign unless you are in complete agreement. 

2.  *The truth in lending act disclosure*. This dictates what the interest rate  charged on the loan is. This is disclosed in the annual percentage rate  box in the upper left-hand corner. This percentage will not match exactly  what is stated on the note due to the way the annual percentage rate is  calculated, but it should be within about half a percentage point. Read  down and look at the schedule of payments. If you agreed to a 30-year  fixed rate loan, there will be 359 payments in one amount and 1 pay 

ment of a slightly different amount. *If there is any deviation from that,  don’t sign*. 

3.  *The note*. That is the formal contract between you and the lender as to  who pays what and when. The terms of the note should be exactly  what was agreed to between you and the loan officer. If you sign the  note and there is a discrepancy, the note will control and the loan officer  will forget there was a discrepancy. Again, once you sign the note, there  are no oral changes to it. What you are looking for is the percentage  rate of the loan and the repayment terms of the loan. If you have a  variable rate loan, you want to pay attention to the index. You do not  want the LIBOR index; you want a Fed funds index. The LIBOR is very  volatile and changes radically. This means your house payment can  change radically. Again, if the note does not state what was agreed,  don’t sign it. 

4.  *The mortgage or deed of trust*. This you can review quickly to simply  make sure that the terms of the mortgage or deed of trust tracks the  terms of the note, and has your address correct. 

Let’s be clear, you are committed when you sign. If what is in the docu ments is not what was agreed to, DON’T SIGN AND WALK AWAY.

**Rule 15: Check for Lender Mistakes 45**   
Rule   
16 

**“It became clear  to me that this  conversation was  not really a**  

**conversation.  I was trying to  explain my case,  and he was not  listening.”**   
**Don’t Keep Explaining**

Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a harder  battle. 

—Plato 

I get calls every day from my mortgage companies.  Even when I told the company that held my second  mortgage that I was in foreclosure, they still asked  me to “pay up and bring my account current.” 

It became clear to me that this conversation was  not really a conversation. I was trying to explain my  case, and he was not listening. His goal was only to  get me to pay up, not to help me deal with my mort 

gage or changing the terms of it. He did not even  refer me to another branch of the bank’s mortgage  department that might actually help me with that.  My conclusion was that if they were calling me, it  probably was for their benefit and not mine\! 

Upon investigation, I found that there was actually  a Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. This act gives  you the debtor some rights and restricts some of  the actions the debt collections company can do.  For example, debt collectors may not: 

•  use threats of violence or harm,   
•  publish a list of consumers who refuse to pay  their debts (except to a credit bureau), 

•  use obscene or profane language, or •  repeatedly use the telephone to annoy  someone. 

Debt collectors may not use any false or mislead ing statements when collecting a debt. They can’t 

**46 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
•  falsely imply that they are attorneys or government representatives, •  falsely imply that you have committed a crime, 

•  falsely represent that they operate or work for a credit bureau, •  misrepresent the amount of your debt, 

•  indicate that papers being sent to you are legal forms when they are  not, or 

•  indicate that papers being sent to you are not legal forms when they  are. 

Debt collectors can’t state that 

•  you will be arrested if you do not pay your debt;   
•  they will seize, garnish, attach, or sell your property or wages, unless the  collection agency or creditor intends to do so, and it is legal to do so; or •  actions, such as a lawsuit, will be taken against you, when such action  legally may not be taken, or when they do not intend to take such  action. 

Debt collectors may not 

•  give false credit information about you to anyone, including a credit  bureau; 

•  send you anything that looks like an official document from a court or  government agency when it is not; or 

•  use a false name. 

Debt collectors may not engage in unfair practices and can’t 

•  collect any amount greater than your debt, unless your state law per mits such a charge; 

•  deposit a postdated check prematurely;   
•  use deception to make you accept collect calls or pay for telegrams; •  take or threaten to take your property unless this can be done legally; or •  contact you by postcard. 

Even though these laws are in place to protect you, they don’t always do  that. For example, our second mortgage (HELOC) is with National City. If  we are a few days late with our payment, they keep calling unmercifully  5–10 times a day. We just unplugged our home phone, I found that is the  best way to deal with this kind of company who has your number on an  automated dialing system.

**Rule 16: Don’t Keep Explaining 47**   
Rule17 

**“Most of the**  

**important**  

**things in the**  

**world have been  accomplished  by people who  have kept on**  

**trying when**  

**there seemed to  be no hope at all”  (Dale Carnegie).**   
**Be Persistent**

The role of the bank, the negotiator, the loan modi fication program, etc. is to collect as much money  from you as they can. They are not on your side. In  every communication you get from the bank, it says  in big letters “WE ARE A DEBT COLLECTOR.” 

They will throw enough roadblocks in your way that  you will feel like Sisyphus (the poor guy from Greek  mythology who toiled all day pushing a big rock up  a hill, only to find in the morning it had rolled down  again, and he has to start all over). Poor Sisyphus  was cursed to do this for eternity. 

In my case, I tried to do the right thing by letting the  bank know right away as soon as my loan rate  adjusted from 5.3% to 7.5% in November of 2007  (and my monthly payment jumped \$1500) that  I would have trouble paying my new mortgage  amount. I got referred to the loss mitigation depart 

ment, and got an 800 number to the Washington  Mutual “care team.” I was then told that I needed to  talk to the loan modification department. After  being transferred three different times, and getting  hung up on twice, I finally talked to an actual human  in this department and explained my situation.  They said they would send me a loan modification  application, but to not be too hopeful, as most peo 

ple did not get a loan modification 

I diligently filled out the form, supplied months of  bank statements, two years of tax returns, a profit  and loss statement (P\&L) for my business and for  my wife’s, and pay stubs to show my wife had been  

**48 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
paid, etc. All told, we sent in a three page application with 106 pages of  backup financial documentation. When I did not hear from WaMu for a  month, I called the “care team” number only to find out that they lost my  application (or had never received it) and had no record of my applying to  the program. 

I was told to go to the WaMu Web site and print out another loan modifica tion application and send it in. I promptly did this, and waited two months  for a response, which I never received. I figured that I needed professional  help with this situation. I went to a local nonprofit who said they dealt with  this situation all the time. The counselor there went over my financials and  helped me fill out the loan modification form again and submit it with  the requested documentation. That was in July 2008\. In October, I got a  request for missing documentation (which we had sent them already), and  the nonprofit counselor sent it in again. 

About that time, I had run out of money, and decided it was better to pay  my health insurance premium than to pay my mortgage. I never did hear  back from the loan modification department, but was notified in early  December that I was in foreclosure. 

I did not take “no” for an answer\! In desperation, I called the CEO of Chase  Manhattan, and talked to someone on his staff, told them my story, and  they said they would look into it. Sure enough a few days later I got a letter  saying that they had looked at my file and denied my application for loan  modification because of too many monthly expenses. 

I was beginning to feel more and more like Sisyphus, and in frustration, the  week before Christmas, I called the CEO again. I did not get to speak to  anyone in person this time, and complained that I had been denied a loan  modification based on old financial data. Sure enough just after Christmas  I got two calls from Washington Mutual asking me to fax in the updated  financial information. Just after the New Year (2009), I did get a letter say 

ing that I was now being considered for their loan modification program, it  would take 30–45 days for a decision and that it did not affect any of terms  of my foreclosure. I figured it was time to get a lawyer, and had no expecta tions that WaMu would do anything but proceed with the foreclosure.  It turns out that you need to watch the bank’s processes also. In my case,  they did not follow the law in notifying me of my foreclosure, and notified  me too early.

**Rule 17: Be Persistent 49**   
Rule18 

**“With the current  credit crunch,  mortgage**  

**companies are  overwhelmed with  applications for  loan modification  and foreclosures;  a situation that  benefits neither  the bank nor the  homeowner.”**   
**Control the**    
**Conversation**

I actually have two mortgage companies. One went  out of business and its assets were acquired by  another financial institution. The other bank is hav ing their own problems and may also go under.  Do you think either of them are worried about me  and my mortgage(s)? Not likely. Do you think that  they have given anyone who calls you on the phone  any information besides your loan number, social  security number, phone number, and how much  you currently owe them? Very likely\! 

Don’t play their game. When they call control the  conversation. When they ask you for money, say  you are not sure they are the institution that owns  their mortgage and that you would like to see the  original loan documents to prove that they are indeed  your mortgage company. State that you are very will 

ing to pay them, but have had others take advantage  of you, and that you need to see these legal docu ments before you can do that. 

They will probably get off the phone confused,  because their call script does not account for this  answer (although it is becoming more common).  Yet, it is your right to see the documents that they  are using to claim that you owe them money. If they  are able to produce the documents (and this can  take months, if they can do it at all), have them  looked at for inconstancies and potential loan viola 

tions by a real-estate law professional. If these are  found, you can use them as leverage against the  mortgage company. 

**50 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
At this point, it is of no use to talk to anyone at the mortgage company that  does not have the ability to negotiate with you. The loan modification  department will not know how to handle this situation and will most likely  bury your application (like what happened to me). It is probably better to  have your lawyer contact the mortgage company’s lawyer directly with the  mortgage infringements and start a negotiation on your behalf. 

Why can’t you go through normal channels? Well, two years ago there  may have been normal channels and a chance you could talk to a man ager or someone in authority. However, today the mortgage companies  are under resourced and incapable of managing the volume of requests  they receive. A tidal wave of foreclosures has washed over them. In some  cases like CountryWide and Washington Mutual, that tidal wave was  enough to drown the company. 

Although these companies are gone, it does not mean that your loan was  not sold to another financial institution. Do you think that institution has a  good handle on your mortgage and is willing to negotiate it with you? Think  again. 

The last time I called Washington Mutual they told me that each loan  negotiator they had (and they did not have nearly enough) had at least 400  loan modification applications to deal with each month. That is almost 20  applications a day, or 2.5 per hour, or one every 17.5 minutes. That means  they have 17.5 minutes to read your file, the many pages of backup docu 

mentation, figure out if you qualify for their program (fit their debt ratios),  draft a letter (or sign a form letter) to you, and then move on to the next file.  How clearly do you think they will look at your specific situation? You can  bet the negotiator’s role, like many other gatekeepers, is to say “NO.” I was  told by a real-estate professional that less than 7% of people who apply  for loan modifications actually get them.

**Rule 18: Control the Conversation 51**   
Rule19 

**“I also realized  that I have**  

**been financially  anorexic, meaning  that I was**  

**unwilling to spend  money on almost  anything,**  

**especially if**  

**it was for myself.”**   
**Take Care of Yourself**

In my case, the process involving the two mortgage  companies I am working with has taken over a 18  months, and it is still not done. I thought it would be  done quite a while ago, and I was wrong. This is a  marathon, not a sprint. The banks have lots of  resources I don’t have, and for them it is a relay  event (they can hand off the calls to other collec 

tions people), whereas it is only me running for my  team. 

The whole process of loan modification is upset ting, and over the last year, I have not been sleeping  regularly, eating well, being financially anorexic (not  willing to spend any money on anything), not taking  a vacation, not giving myself any time off from my  business, and not getting regular exercise. I was  depressed and sad about my situation and was  often taking on too much work to distract myself  from my financial problems. I was not paying my  wife the attention she deserved, and I was not clear  that my clients (from my analyst and consulting  business) were getting my best. 

In addition, I was ashamed to talk about the situa tion with anyone but my wife. The calls from the  collections people did nothing to help my situation  and only made me feel more ashamed and like the  deadbeat they thought I was. As one thing piled on  top of another, and the situation dragged on and  on, I started talking about the situation with my fam ily and a few selected friends. 

**52 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
Once I realized that this was going to take a while, I needed to come up  with a plan that helped me through the marathon because I was deter mined to finish. I may not be able to determine how long it will take, but I  am committed to a positive outcome. 

Here is the plan I made for myself to help take care of myself during the  rest of the process with the bank. My goal is to emerge from this process  whole and happy, not an emotional and physical wreck. 

•  Walk 3–4 miles 3–4 times a week (usually with a partner for motivation  and conversation). 

•  Be careful about what I eat, less processed foods and more fruits and  vegetables. 

•  Be willing to talk about my situation and eliminate the power my shame  has over me. 

•  Spend a bit on myself, I am worth it, and the bank is not going to break  my door in just because I take my wife out for dinner on Valentine’s  Day. 

•  Unplug my home phone to avoid the harassing calls by the collections  people. When they call me at work, just say that it is our policy that our  employees can’t take personal calls at work. They managed to get my  cell phone number from me (a mistake on my part), but I downloaded a  special ring that is “silent” and attached it to the bank’s phone number,  so that when they call my cell phone does not ring. 

•  Talk to my doctor about what I can do about my sleeplessness and  depression. 

•  Listen to the support I am getting from my friends and family, take it in,  and realize I am a worthwhile person and not the deadbeat the collec tions people think I am.

**Rule 19: Take Care of Yourself 53**   
Rule   
20 

**“Once I was**  

**willing to talk  about my**  

**situation and got  over some of my  shame about it.  I planned a ‘last  party in our**  

**house’ and sent  out hundreds of  invitations.”**   
**Celebrate the Little  Victories**

Dealing with the loan modification process could  literally drive you crazy. One of the strategies I  found to help counteract these tendencies was to  celebrate any little victory that occurred. I cele 

brated when 

•  I got confirmation my loan modification applica tion and the 80 pages of supporting documenta tion was received 

•  A lawyer (Craig Triance) was willing to take my  case (they only take cases they think they have a  good chance of winning). 

•  My call to Chase Manhattan’s CEO had resulted  in a response from Washington Mutual •  I got notification I was in my lender’s loan modifi cation program (after four applications) •  Both of my mortgage lenders had done things  wrong in the mortgage initiation process that  would allow me to sue them for the full value of  the house (but more likely to use as leverage in a  loan modification program) 

•  My first mortgage lender had put a three-week  moratorium on foreclosures (to give the U.S.  treasury department time to explain their stimu lus plan, and the role the bank would play in it) 

•  My publisher decided that this book was very  timely and put it on the fast track for publication 

My celebrations did not always have to cost money.  I am not suggesting that you pop open a bottle of  Louis Roderer Cristal (\$300 per bottle) for each lit tle victory. Sometimes, my celebration was just tak ing some quiet time for myself and enjoying the  

**54 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
feeling of satisfaction I got from these small victories, before charging  back into the fray. 

Once I was willing to talk about my situation and got over some of my  shame about it. I planned a “last party in our house” party and sent out  hundreds of invitations. Not only was it an invitation, but it gave a quick  explanation of our situation, to let people know that we were celebrating  the good times we had in this house over the last 21 years. We invited our  friends to come and celebrate with us. 

Another way I celebrated was to be thankful for each new day I had in our  house (gratitude). Our house is nothing special. It is an old farm house  (built in 1904\) and still needs lots of work, but over the years I have had a  lot of work done on the house and have customized it so that it works for  my lifestyle. 

I have been thinking of another party to have and another celebration.  This one is about removing the clutter. After 21 years, it is amazing the  amount of stuff we have accumulated in the house and office. Getting 20  or so friends to help go through this stuff and either give it away or mark it  for a garage sale sounds like a good excuse for another party. Just the fact  of uncluttering my house (in preparation for moving if/when we get thrown  out) is a good way to start to help in the uncluttering of my life.

**Rule 20: Celebrate the Little Victories 55**   
Rule   
21 

**“By failure, it  means that the  loan goes back**  

**into foreclosure,  and the lender  gets the house  anyway.”**   
**Make Yourself a Better  Candidate**

As you negotiate with your lender, assume their  mindset is to not make a deal. It is simpler to get to  no than it is to get to yes. 

The reason for this is very straightforward. Some thing over 50% of the loan modifications, forbear ance agreements, or foreclosure prevention efforts  end in failure. By failure, it means that the loan goes  back into foreclosure, and the lender gets it any way. With the odds so low, why even try to negotiate  something other than a foreclosure—at least this  way you are going to get your collateral back on a  specific date. 

So shift the tables on the negotiator. Use your dis cussions with the negotiator to explain why you are  a good candidate for relief. 

Some points to use when preparing your hardship  letter or in negotiation: 

•  Concentrate on explaining why you need help,  and cannot make your payments at the current  rate. 

•  Do not concentrate on why the situation hap pened. The negotiators are largely immune, at  this point, to hard luck stories. Don’t mean to be  callous about this, but that is reality. 

•  Write in the first person about your situation.  Don’t use a form letter, don’t quote from Barak  Obama. Simple concise English—delivered at  8th grade level. Focus on making sure the lender  retains an income stream from you, whatever  that is. 

**56 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
•  Don’t make threats. Threatening anything from litigation to a nerve gas  attack on corporate headquarters is counterproductive and will only  result in having your request denied. 

•  Make sure the math works. Most of the lenders now run you through an  assessment matrix to see if your numbers make sense. If they do, you  will get a modification. If they do not, they will not help you. More and  more banks are shifting to the mathematical mode. 

•  Be specific. Explain what you want and why, and be succinct. The per son reviewing your file for the lender will consider your file for 15–20  minutes tops. And the decision on you and your house will be made in  that time. Do their jobs for them. Tell them what you want and why. 

•  Include a household budget. Concentrate on the big ticket items—mort gages, car payments, credit cards, and utilities. Nobody wants to know  what your dry cleaning bill is. The banks understand you need to eat  and budget in a food allowance. No need to include the number of times  you eat at Burger King per month. 

•  In the household budget, do not underreport income. If your hours have  been cut, or there is no more overtime, state this, but be accurate. •  Check the Internet or a local realtor about the decline in housing prices  in your area. A decline in value alone is not sufficient reason to obtain a  loan workout. But it does give the bank the sense that if they take the  property back, they are in for a beating, and will lose a substantial por tion of their investment if they take the property back. This is particularly  effective in dealing with property in perceived high-value states such as  the Northeast, Florida, and California. Showing they will get only one third of their investment value may give them pause, and you an angle  to keep your house.

**Rule 21: Make Yourself a Better Candidate 57**   
Rule   
22 

**“Most of the**  

**people you talk to  from the**  

**mortgage**  

**company can’t  help you, they  don’t have the**  

**knowledge or  authority, and  their job is to say  ‘No’ to you.”**   
**Always Go to the Top**

The role of a “gatekeeper” is usually to keep people  out. Most of the people you talk to at a mortgage  company these days fall into two categories: gate keepers or collectors. Collections people often don’t  know any more than your loan number, social secu rity number, and the amount you currently owe on  your loan. If these people call, don’t engage them in  conversation, it is a no win situation. Even if you ask  to speak to a supervisor, you will probably get a  slightly better trained person, who may have worked  for the mortgage company for a few more months  (turnover is really high with employees right now)  then the original person you talked with. 

In my case, being the stubborn type I tried to deal  with these people for months and finally realized  I could not win at their game. I had no leverage. So  I unplugged my home phone and out of frustration  called the CEO/chairman of the board for Chase  Manhattan (which had acquired Washington  Mutual last summer). I figured I would probably  never get through, and if I did, he would not be  there, be in a meeting, or not willing to listen. I was  wrong\! Not, I never did talk with the Chase Man hattan CEO but I did talk with someone on his staff.  She evidently called someone in charge at Wash 

ington Mutual, because my loan application, which  had languished for six months, all of a sudden had  some action taken on it. 

I was contacted by a negotiator from Washington  Mutual who was handling my case. Of course,  

**58 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
since the loan negotiator’s role is that of a gatekeeper, he said “no” to my  loan modification, and hoped that was the end of it. However, since I am  in a position of “You are going to take my house anyway, I have no credit  rating left, there is not much more you can do to me, so what do I have to  lose, I can try anything I can think of, it could not get worse\!” 

OK, so I called the Chase Manhattan CEO again complaining that I got an  instant refusal for my loan modification, and that Washington Mutual has  sat on the application so long that the financial information had now  changed. Sure enough, two days later, I not only got a call from the guy  who ran the negotiator department at Washington Mutual (obviously he  got a call from his Chase Manhattan boss) asking for the new financial  information, which I promptly faxed into them. 

I did get a letter back acknowledging the fact that they were reviewing my  application for loan modification and that it would take 45 days before they  would get back to me. Given this timeframe my house would already be  auctioned off in a foreclosure sale before the negotiator got back to me,  so essentially what they were saying was “no” again. Like the collectors,  it was a losing situation to play the negotiators game, and the only way I  could win was to change the game. 

I needed more leverage. So I contacted Craig Triance (my coauthor) and  a real-estate lawyer who has a lot of experience with this sort of situation.  Yes, it did cost me more money, but as the mortgagee you get to pay for  everything (read your mortgage contract) not only your lawyer, but also the  bank’s lawyer.

**Rule 22: Always Go to the Top 59**   
Rule   
23 

**“If it sounds too  good to be true it  probably is\!”**   
**Get Help When You  Need It**

I am a smart and well-educated guy. Unfortunately,  my schooling was more in neurobiology and psy chology rather than banking and real estate. I have  only done one real-estate transaction in my life and  that one was not going so well now. 

For me realizing I could not do everything in my  best interest in this mortgage situation was the first  step in my learning to ask for help from a variety of  sources 

**Professional Help** 

I am neither a bookkeeper nor an accountant, al though my wife is a bookkeeper. When we filled out  our loan modification application for the third time,  we were being too conservative with our expenses  and ended up counting some of them twice, once  on our loan modification application and once in  the P\&L I needed to submit because I am a sole  proprietor.  

One of the people looking at our application saw  immediately that our expenses were out of whack  and too high for the dollars we were bringing in for  a two-person household. She did a forensic audit  where she dug into all of the numbers on both doc 

uments (and believe me we got several calls asking  us to verify specific expenses). Because she had  an accounting background (as well as real estate)  she was able to find about \$3000 in expenses that  

**60 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
were double booked (i.e., they appeared both on the P\&L and the loan  application). We probably would have never caught that ourselves, but the  professional we worked with did. 

Other professional help is coming from our lawyer in navigating this tortur ous system. It was very hard for me to pay for a lawyer to help me with this  situation because: (1) we had already been ripped off by a Florida loan  modification company for \$2850, and (2) why should I have to pay a lawyer  to work out a loan where the best outcome would be I would be paying for  my house for the rest of my life (and getting to live in it). 

I got help from doctors to help with my mood and weight issues and my  psychological well-balance (a short-term solution). 

I had a friend who is a local real-estate professional find out what my  house is really worth by looking at recent sales of similar houses in our  area. She actually came by to talk with my wife and I and counsel us on  our options (i.e., short sale, etc.). 

We had a professional appraiser come look at our house and tell us the  value in a report (in January of 2008 it was worth \$1.1 million, a year later  it was worth \$900,000 and dropping). 

Getting referred to mortgage brokers and candidly discussing our options  at this point. When we tried to do a refinance about two years ago, we went  through five different mortgage brokers (only two of them are still in busi ness), and were unsuccessful in getting refinanced. 

**Nonprofessional Help** 

•  Enlisting friends and family for support   
•  Having many friends point me towards resources I might have never  found on the Internet 

•  Friends that dragged me away from my computer and to go out for a  walk, a meal, or a movie 

•  Family that were outraged by the situation (who could not help finan cially) and tried everything they could think of to help me in this situation  (even calling their own mortgage brokers to get advice for me) 

Don’t be too proud to accept help, especially if it is given with an open  heart. Be wary of those who offer the moon. I have had loan modification  companies tell me that they could work out my loan in a month and that  they had gotten settlements for other clients where they were paying 1%  interest on a fixed rate for 40 years, and had been forgiven the amount  they were delinquent on their mortgage. If it sounds too good to be true it  probably is.

**Rule 23: Get Help When You Need It 61**   
Rule   
24 

**“He said that he  had to hold the  house in his name  for at least a year  or two (or the**  

**second mortgage  would come due),  before he could  sell it back to me.”**   
**Question Your**    
**Assumptions**

It is better to have enough ideas for some of them  to be wrong, than to be always right by having no  ideas at all. 

—Edward De Bono 

Creativity is all about questioning your assump tions. Is that real, is that true? What if it was like  this? Why not let your house go into foreclosure to  save it? That is one of the questions an investor  posed to me on the phone one day. I had been so  focused on fighting the foreclosure that I forgot to  question the assumptions. 

What would that look like I said? He explained the  process to me the best he could (as he was driving  in his car). If the trustee puts my property up for  sale on the San Francisco court house steps, the  bank(s) would want at least \$700,000 for it which  would put it out of many investor’s reach, and so he  speculated that the bank would get no takers at this  price. If they were authorized to go lower, this inves 

tor would be in the audience and when the price got  down to about \$500,000, he would bid on it. Since  he speculated that this would be the only bid on the  property, he would probably win the bid. 

This he said would get rid of the second mortgage  and pay off the bank for the first. Since he got the  property at a reduced price he could lease it back  to me for about the \$2500/month I was originally  paying for my mortgage. This all sounded great to  me, the only catch was he did not want to take all  the risk, and asked me to come up with at least  

**62 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
\$100,000. If I had that kind of money I would not be in foreclosure I said?  They only asked me for about \$30,000 to get me out of foreclosure.  Obviously he was thinking about this from an investor’s perspective and  not a homeowner’s. But he was responding to my request to figure out a  way to stay in my home. 

So the first problem was to find someone with \$100,000 that wanted to  invest in my house. The second problem was, how could the investor be  sure he would win the bid for my house and at the reduced price of  \$500,000. From his experience he told me, he had done lots of these and  that is just the way things went. 

I thought about this for a while and rejected the idea, as it had all of the  worst possibilities for me. I would have a foreclosure on my credit record.  If the investor bought the house, how long was he willing to hold it, as his  money would be tied up, even though my monthly payment would cover  his mortgage payment for the house. He really did not make any serious  money until he sold the house for a much higher price. He could wait for  the market to go up, and thus his equity in the house would rise and he  would be able to capitalize on that through sale of the house. 

However, not only did I want to live in the house but I also wanted to own  it. He said that he had to hold the house in his name for at least a year or  two (or the second mortgage would come due), before he could sell it back  to me. In the mean time, I had to come up with a way to pay the person who  invested the \$100,000 in the house, as well as restoring my credit enough  to get a loan (mortgage) to purchase the house back. How much chance  was there of that with a foreclosure on my record? Not much I thought, but  it was an interesting idea, and very creative; he was questioning all the  assumptions\!

**Rule 24: Question Your Assumptions 63**   
Rule   
25 

**“In the old days,  you signed the  note, and the note  was then taken by  the bank and**  

**placed in a vault  somewhere.”**   
**Ask them to Produce  the Note**

Anybody who has ever seen an episode of CSI can  follow along on this one. You are just connecting  the dots. 

Implied in the ability of a bank to foreclose on your  house, or collect payments from you, for that mat ter, is that they have the legal right to do so. We are  starting to find out that is not necessarily the case  in some situations. 

Of all the documents that you signed, there are  only two that really matter: (1) the note and (2) the  mortgage or deed of trust. The note is your written  agreement to repay the bank, and what the rules  and procedures are for doing so. The mortgage or  deed of trust assigns the note to a particular chunk  of real estate, typically your house. The right to  payment depends upon who holds the note, since  that is the promise you made to pay. 

In the old days, you signed the note, and the note  was then taken by the bank and placed in a vault  somewhere. The bank then sent you a payment  reminder each month for the term of the note.  When the note was fully paid off, it was marked paid  in full and mailed back to you as proof of full satis 

faction of the note. 

With the creation of mortgage-backed securities,  that simple concept changed a lot. Your note now  goes through a prolonged journey Moses would be  proud of. It went from where you signed it back  to the notary, then to the mortgage broker, then to  the wholesaler, then to the warehouse line, and on  

**64 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
and on. The end result was that the note did not necessarily end up with  the person you have been making your payments to. It may have in fact  wound up in a storage bin in Omaha. Or, equally possibly, no one knows  where it is. 

This problem first surfaced in Cleveland, Ohio during the first round of  sub-prime foreclosures in 2007\. Ohio law requires lenders to sue to start  a foreclosure, and they must prove they hold the note to do so. Ohio state  court judges started noticing that many banks were foreclosing without  being able to produce the note. After being politely asked to produce the  note on several occasions, the banks were still unable to do so. So judges  started dismissing foreclosure cases. 

Other judges in other states, notably Florida, which has rules similar to  Ohio, took note and started seeing the same thing—banks could not pro duce notes. The problem is not just confined to Florida and Ohio. The  problem is everywhere. 

So when you are facing a foreclosure action, don’t roll up into a ball on the  floor. Fight back. Hit the bank where they are most vulnerable. Do a  demand for production of documents and demand they produce the note.  My guess is many times they will not. They will produce an “affidavit of lost  note” instead. Make their lives miserable and demand the affiant of the  note (an affiant is the person who is stating under penalty of perjury that  the note is lost) be produced in court. Judges are becoming increasingly  sympathetic to this argument. The pitch is simple: banks are losing money  they would just use on bonuses and junkets, and you are losing your  house. 

If you do get the affiant on the stand, Appendix F contains a list of ques tions you may want to ask the person. You will be quite surprised by the  answers you get to some of these questions. Don’t worry so much about  lying; staring a judge or jury in the face and telling whopper is a rare skill.

**Rule 25: Ask them to Produce the Note 65**   
**Section 3: Options,**    
**Solutions, and**    
**Resolution**

This last section is a set of rules that helps you look    
at your options, however few they may be. Maybe    
there are some options for you that you did not    
know about (and the bank will not tell you). How do    
you get “leverage” on the bank? How do you get out    
with only losing your shirt and not your pants? What    
to let go of (credit score), what not to touch (retire   
ment account), and which loans to stay away from    
(HELOC). We believe this section’s rules will not    
only give you more options, and make you a more    
knowledgeable homeowner, but better able to take    
care of yourself when interacting with your bank. 

**66 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
**Section 3: Options, Solutions, and Resolution 67**  
Rule   
26 

**“As I am fond of  saying ‘banks are  only willing to  lend you money  when you DON’T  need it.’ ”**   
**Look at Some of Your  Options**

This was a tough rule to write because not only did  it force me out of any denial about possibly losing  my house, but it also made me look at the quickly  limiting options I had, the closer my house got to  auction in foreclosure. Since real estate was not my  field of expertise, I was willing to talk to anyone and  did talk to many of those that sent me solicitations  for their services through the mail. I actually learned  a lot about my options through those conversations  and have listed the options as I have come to under stand them below: 

**Lender mediation:** This is what I am currently try ing to do through the loan modification process  with Washington Mutual (JP Morgan/Chase). 

**Restructuring the loan (lender):** Here the len der agrees to restructure the loan, maybe the loan  amount (because your house value is less than the  loan value), or the loan rate (because it has adjusted  up to rates significantly higher than the rest of the  market), or the term of the loan (most loans are for  30 years, but lenders are now looking at 40-year  terms to get your monthly payment down). 

**Refinance your home:** A new mortgage usually at  a lower rate or monthly payment (not much of that  possible today with the changing policies for  refinances). As I am fond of saying “banks are  only willing to lend you money when you DON’T  need it.” 

**68 42 Rules for Saving Your House from Foreclosure**   
**Putting your home up for sale:** This is either through a “HelpUSell” type  organization, or through a local realtor. The HelpUSell option costs you  less in terms of commission, and a realtor will charge a 5%–6% commis sion for selling your house (they have to split that with the other realtor who  is representing the buyer, as well as the company they work for, so they are  not getting all of it). So let’s do the math: If you home is worth (and sells  for) \$1 million, the realtor pockets \$60,000 of whatever profit you made on  that home. If it is through a HelpUSell type organization, the cost would be  more like \$10,000. 

The difference here is motivation, and the amount of time you have. If you  are already in foreclosure, you need a very motivated realtor to sell your  house quickly—often if you tell the lender you are selling your house (and  show them the listing) they will suspend foreclosure (as they get more  money if you are able to sell your house); however, they will not suspend  foreclosure forever, so you need to get your house sold FAST\! 

**Getting a bridge loan:** I had only heard of this in terms of my client com panies that are start-ups and had gotten a first round of venture capital  funding and were working on securing a second round, but projected that  at their current spending rate they would run out of money before the  round was completed and they got their new funding. Often their current  lenders would give them a bridge loan to tide them over until the new fund ing came through. No loans come without a price, and in the case of a  homeowner they might get a bridge loan to pay back the bank payments  they owe on their house to get it out of foreclosure (however, the rates for  these loans are often much higher than the going mortgage rate, both  because they are shorter term and higher risk for the lender (what hap pens if the future loan does not come through). 

The next three rules (27–29) look at the some more options for those with  a mortgage in foreclosure. There are probably more options than you  think, so keep an open mind as you read through these rules. What I found  helpful for me was to not dismiss any of the options right off but to sit with  the option and see how it felt to me. Was it really what I wanted? What are  some of the consequences of choosing this option? Like me, maybe you  need some help in choosing the right option for your situation.

**Rule 26: Look at Some of Your Options 69**   
Rule   
27 

**“In many cases,  when the**  

**homeowner can’t  get the bank to  negotiate with  them on loan  amounts, terms,  or interest rates,  they write off any  investment they  had in the house  and walk away  from it,**  

**abandoning the  house.”**   
**Consider Investors,  Partnerships, and  Lease Options**

Rule 26 took a hard look at some options for a per son in your situation (in foreclosure or close to it).  However, those are not all the options you have: 

**Sell to an Investor:** This is often a way to get out  of your home quickly, and works best if you still  have equity in your house. Let’s say your house is  worth \$1 million (either appraised value or from  comparable multiple listings). Your loan totals  \$700,000, which means you have \$300,000 in  equity, or so you thought\! An investor is willing to  buy your house now, without any fixing it up or, sales  costs, but at a 20% discount, so they would buy it  for \$800,000, you get the \$100,000 you still have  left in equity and agree to the sales terms with the  investor (you need to vacate the house in 30 or 60  days, etc.), the investor (which often is a syndicate  of people) will come in, fix up the house, and turn  around and sell it for \$1–1.1 million, making a tidy  profit of several hundred thousand dollars (usually  within a year or two). 

If you don’t have any equity left in your home, this  is a much harder process. Let’s say your house was  worth \$700,000 when you bought it, and you got a  mortgage for \$500,000. Since then the area where  your house is in has dropped in value rapidly  (maybe you are in Stockton, California) and you get  your house appraised two years after you bought it  (so you have paid off nothing but interest on your  mortgage) and the current value is \$485, 000,  \$15,000 less than the mortgage for the house.
